immediate: Move them to one room with fresh air and a separate toilet or bucket
Pick one caregiver; use gloves and a mask for close care
Put soap or sanitizer at the room door
then: Disinfect touched surfaces daily and log vital signs twice a day
Get emergency care for breathing trouble, confusion, or no urine

title: Nutrition in Long Emergencies - Deficiencies to Watch For
summary: Stored staples like white rice, flour, sugar, and canned food can keep you full but leave you short of key vitamins after weeks or months. Learn the early signs of scurvy, beriberi, and other deficiencies and how to prevent them.

steps.title: Understand why long emergencies cause deficiencies
steps.body: In a short emergency, calories and water are what matter. After about a month on a narrow diet, missing vitamins start to show. The risk is highest when meals are mostly polished white rice, white flour, sugar, and fats, with little fresh produce, whole grains, beans, or meat. Long storage, canning, and heavy cooking destroy some vitamins, especially vitamin C. Children, pregnant and breastfeeding women, older adults, heavy drinkers, and people with long-lasting diarrhea are most at risk.

steps.title: Plan a varied store, not just calories
steps.body: Build food storage around variety: whole grains (brown rice, oats, whole wheat), dried beans and lentils, canned fish and meat, peanut butter and nuts, canned or dried fruit and vegetables, powdered milk, and fortified cereals. Add a bottle of a basic daily multivitamin for each person, rotated before its expiration date. Store seeds for sprouting and fast-growing greens. See the food storage and rationing guides for calorie planning.

steps.title: Watch for scurvy (vitamin C)
steps.body: The body cannot make or store much vitamin C. Signs usually appear after at least a month of very low intake and often take about three months. Early signs are fatigue, weakness, irritability, poor appetite, and aching legs. Later signs include swollen, bleeding gums, easy bruising and small bleeding spots on the skin (often on the legs), corkscrew-shaped hairs, slow wound healing, sore swollen joints, and anemia. MedlinePlus notes older adults with poor nutrition are most often affected. Adults need roughly 75 to 90 mg a day.

steps.title: Prevent and correct scurvy
steps.body: Good vitamin C sources include sweet peppers, citrus, kiwi, berries, tomatoes, potatoes, broccoli, cabbage, Brussels sprouts, and leafy greens. Eat them raw or lightly cooked when you can, since cooking and long storage lower vitamin C. Sprouted seeds and fresh wild greens you can identify with certainty also help (see the edible plants guides). Vitamin C tablets store well and are a cheap insurance item - follow the label. When vitamin C is restored, aches and fatigue often improve within days, while bruising and bleeding can take weeks.

steps.title: Watch for beriberi (thiamine, vitamin B1)
steps.body: A diet mostly of polished white rice, white flour, or sugar - a classic stored-food diet - can cause thiamine deficiency. Heavy alcohol use, long diarrhea, fever, hard physical work, pregnancy, and breastfeeding raise the need. Early signs are vague: tiredness, irritability, poor memory, poor appetite, and weight loss. Later come tingling or burning feet, leg cramps, and weakness ('dry' beriberi), or a fast heartbeat, leg swelling, and shortness of breath from heart strain ('wet' beriberi). Confusion with unsteady walking and eye problems can be Wernicke encephalopathy, a medical emergency.

steps.title: Prevent beriberi
steps.body: Thiamine is in whole grains, enriched flour and cereals, pork, liver and other meats, beans and other legumes, nuts, potatoes, and yeast. Choose enriched or whole-grain staples over plain polished rice where possible, mix beans into rice meals, and limit alcohol. Breastfed babies can develop beriberi if the mother is deficient, so nursing mothers need a good diet or a supplement.

steps.title: Know the other common gaps
steps.body: Iron deficiency causes tiredness, pale skin, and shortness of breath, especially in women and children - meat, beans, and fortified cereals help. Little sunlight and no dairy can cause low vitamin D and calcium. A diet mostly of untreated corn can cause pellagra (niacin), with rash on sun-exposed skin, diarrhea, and confusion. Night blindness can be an early sign of vitamin A deficiency - orange vegetables, leafy greens, eggs, and liver help. A daily multivitamin covers much of this, but food variety is the real fix.

steps.title: Track and get help
steps.body: Weigh household members weekly if you can, and watch children's growth, energy, and mood. Note any bleeding gums, unusual bruising, swelling, numbness, or night blindness. These signs can also come from other illnesses, so report them to a clinician when one is reachable. Severe malnutrition, especially in children, needs medical refeeding - restarting large amounts of food too fast after starvation can be dangerous.

warnings: Confusion, unsteady walking, and abnormal eye movements in a poorly fed person or heavy drinker may be thiamine-related brain injury - an emergency.
Restarting full meals too quickly after weeks of starvation can cause dangerous shifts in body salts; get medical guidance for severe malnutrition.
Do not take large doses of vitamin A or iron supplements beyond the label - too much is toxic, especially for children and in pregnancy.
Only eat wild plants you can identify with complete certainty.
proTips: Sprouting lentils, mung beans, or alfalfa in a jar gives fresh vitamin C in a few days with almost no space.
Rotate stored multivitamins and vitamin C each year.
Potatoes and cabbage store for months and still carry useful vitamin C.
Mix brown and white rice to stretch whole-grain stores.

immediate: Add a vitamin C source daily - fresh produce, sprouts, or tablets

title: Glasses, Contacts, Hearing Aids, and Assistive Devices - Backups and Care
summary: If you rely on glasses, contacts, hearing aids, a cane, a walker, or a wheelchair, losing it in a disaster can be as disabling as an injury. Keep backups, power, and repair supplies, and care for devices safely when water and power are short.

steps.title: Inventory every device in the household
steps.body: List each device: glasses (with your current prescription written down), contact lenses and solution, hearing aids or cochlear implant processors and their battery type, dentures, canes, walkers, wheelchairs, braces, communication boards, and any powered equipment. Note the model, the supplier's phone number, and how it is powered. Ready.gov advises older adults and people with disabilities to plan how they will keep assistive devices with them during an evacuation, and to include batteries and chargers in their supply kit.

steps.title: Keep a spare pair of glasses
steps.body: Store your previous pair of glasses or a cheap backup pair made to your current prescription in a hard case in the go-bag, plus a second pair in the car. Add a small screwdriver repair kit, a microfiber cloth, and a strap to keep glasses from falling off. If you wear reading glasses, store several pairs - they are cheap. Prescription sunglasses protect eyes from glare and debris during cleanup.

steps.title: Handle contact lenses safely - or switch to glasses
steps.body: FDA says never to expose contact lenses to any water - tap, bottled, distilled, lake, or ocean - because water can carry germs that cause serious, sight-threatening eye infections. Do not top off old solution or reuse it; empty the case, rinse it with fresh solution, and let it air dry each time. If you cannot wash and dry your hands, have no fresh solution, or the area is dusty or smoky, take the lenses out and wear glasses instead. Daily disposable lenses are a good emergency option. Remove lenses and contact an eye professional for eye pain, redness, blurry vision, or light sensitivity.

steps.title: Keep hearing aids powered and found
steps.body: Store spare hearing aid batteries (a few months' supply), and if your aids are rechargeable, a charger that runs from a power bank or car USB. Consider keeping an older backup hearing aid in your emergency supplies. Connecticut's public health department advises keeping hearing aids in the same secure spot every night - such as a container tied to the nightstand - so you can find them fast in the dark. Store aids in a dry box or with desiccant in humid conditions. Carry a pen and paper or a card that says you are hard of hearing and how best to communicate with you.

steps.title: Plan for mobility devices
steps.body: Keep a folding cane or a spare walker you can grab quickly. For wheelchairs, store a patch kit, pump, and basic tools, and know the chair's weight and whether it folds for transport. Power wheelchairs and scooters need a charging plan: know the battery type and charge time, and ask about a manual backup chair. Practice your evacuation route with the device, including stairs or curbs. Tell your support network how to safely help you move.

steps.title: Protect powered medical devices
steps.body: For anything that plugs in - power chairs, hearing aid chargers, electronic magnifiers, communication devices - keep charged power banks or a portable power station and a car charger. Charge everything when a storm or outage is forecast. Label each device and charger with your name and phone number. Register with your utility as a medical-needs customer if you use life-sustaining equipment.

steps.title: Get replacements after a loss
steps.body: If a device is lost or damaged, tell shelter staff or emergency managers right away; many relief agencies help replace glasses, hearing aid batteries, canes, and wheelchairs. Have copies of your eyeglass prescription, device serial numbers, and insurance cards (Medicare, Medicaid, or others) in your go-bag. Keep a photo of each device and its label on your phone.

warnings: Never rinse or store contact lenses in water of any kind, and never use saliva - it can cause a blinding eye infection.
Eye pain, redness, or blurred vision in a contact lens wearer needs prompt care from an eye professional.
Button batteries for hearing aids are deadly if a child swallows one - store them locked away and seek emergency care immediately if swallowed.
Do not try to repair a power wheelchair's electrical system with improvised parts.
proTips: Tape a copy of your eyeglass prescription inside your glasses case.
A cheap headlamp helps people with low vision move safely at night.
Practice saying or writing your communication needs before an emergency.
Keep hearing aid batteries in their original packaging until use; they last longer.

whenNotTo: Do not keep wearing contact lenses in smoky, dusty, or dirty conditions when you cannot clean your hands; switch to glasses.

immediate: Grab backup glasses, hearing aid batteries, and chargers
Switch from contacts to glasses if you cannot wash hands or lack fresh solution
Keep devices in one known spot at night

Report lost devices to shelter staff for replacement help

title: Older Adults' Health in Emergencies - Heat, Cold, Dehydration, Falls, and Medications
summary: Older adults are hit hardest by heat waves, cold homes, dehydration, falls, and missed medicines during outages. Use these checks and habits to keep an older family member or neighbor safe, or to protect yourself.

steps.title: Build a support network and plan
steps.body: Ready.gov advises older adults to build a network of family, friends, and neighbors who will check in during an emergency. At least one person should have a spare key, know where supplies and medicines are, and know how to use any medical equipment. Keep copies of Medicare, Medicaid, and other insurance cards in the go-bag. Ask any clinic that provides routine treatment about its emergency plan, and line up a backup provider. Plan transportation in advance if you cannot drive or walk far.

steps.title: Protect against heat
steps.body: CDC explains that older bodies adjust poorly to sudden heat, chronic illness changes how the body handles it, and some medicines reduce sweating or temperature control. Drink more water than usual, before feeling thirsty. Spend hot hours in air conditioning - a cooling center, library, or friend's home if yours has no power. Do not rely on a fan alone in extreme heat. Take cool showers or use cool, wet cloths, wear loose light clothing, and avoid using the stove. If your doctor limits fluids or prescribes water pills, ask now how much to drink in hot weather.

steps.title: Check in twice a day during heat
steps.body: CDC advises caregivers to visit older adults at least twice a day during heat and ask: are they drinking enough, do they have a cool place, do they know how to stay cool, and do they show signs of heat illness? Watch for muscle cramps, headache, nausea, vomiting, dizziness, confusion, or unusual tiredness and seek medical care right away for these. Hot, dry or very red skin, confusion, or passing out may be heatstroke - call 911 and cool the person immediately.

steps.title: Protect against cold
steps.body: NIH's National Institute on Aging warns that older adults can develop hypothermia even indoors in a mildly cool home of 60 to 65 F, and advises keeping the thermostat at 68 to 70 F or higher when possible. In an outage, gather everyone in one small room, dress in layers with a hat, use blankets, and eat warm meals and drinks. Some medicines, including some OTC cold remedies, and conditions like diabetes reduce the body's response to cold. Warning signs include confusion or sleepiness, slurred speech, shivering or stiffness, and clumsy movements. A body temperature of 96 F or lower means call 911.

steps.title: Prevent dehydration
steps.body: The sense of thirst weakens with age, and many older adults drink less to avoid trips to a dark or distant toilet. Set out a measured water bottle each morning and track it. Offer fluids at every meal and visit. Watch for dark urine, dry mouth, dizziness when standing, new confusion, and constipation. Treat diarrhea or vomiting early with oral rehydration solution. Sudden confusion in an older adult is a warning sign - check for dehydration, infection, low blood sugar, and heat or cold first, and get care.

steps.title: Prevent falls in a dark, cluttered home
steps.body: CDC reports that about 1 in 4 older adults falls each year, and falls are the leading cause of injury for people 65 and older. Outages and debris make it worse. Put battery or motion-sensor lights along the path to the bathroom and on stairs, and keep a flashlight within reach of the bed. Clear cords, rugs, and clutter from walkways. Wear supportive, non-slip, closed-toe shoes - not loose slippers. Get up slowly and pause before walking. Keep canes and walkers at the right height and within reach. Never climb on chairs; ask for help.

steps.title: Keep medicines on track
steps.body: Older adults often take many medicines, and a missed or doubled dose can be dangerous. Use a weekly pill organizer and a printed list of every medicine, dose, and time. Keep at least a 7 to 14 day reserve. Store medicines in the coolest dry spot during outages, and see the insulin guide for refrigerated medicines. Ask a pharmacist which medicines raise heat or fall risk. Never stop heart, blood pressure, or seizure medicines suddenly without advice.

steps.title: Know when to move them
steps.body: Move an older adult to a cooling or warming center, a relative's home, or a shelter early if the home cannot be kept safely warm or cool, if powered medical equipment cannot run, or if no one can check on them daily. Bring the medicine list, medicines, glasses, hearing aids, dentures, mobility aids, and chargers.

warnings: Heatstroke (hot skin, confusion, collapse) is an emergency - call 911 and cool the person immediately.
A body temperature of 96 F or lower in an older adult means call 911.
Sudden confusion in an older adult is a medical warning sign, not normal aging.
Never use a gas oven, grill, or generator indoors for heat - carbon monoxide kills.
proTips: Use the CDC HeatRisk forecast by ZIP code to plan check-ins on hot days.
Put a night light and a whistle at the bedside of anyone at risk of falls.
Make a large-print card with medicines, allergies, and emergency contacts.
Arrange a buddy check-in by phone or in person at set times each day.

immediate: Check on them at least twice a day
Get them to a cool or warm place and push fluids
Light the path to the bathroom and clear trip hazards
then: Keep medicines on schedule with an organizer and list
